entry.title: A Good Day Out Around Amsterdam
entry.excerpt: A thoughtful guide to riding around Amsterdam, from the IJ and Waterland to the Amstel, Zaanse Schans and the North Sea coast.

children.text: At half past eight on a clear Saturday morning, the ferry from Centraal slipped across the IJ and a woman beside me steadied her coffee with one hand while holding her child's handlebars with the other. On the far bank, Amsterdam Noord was still shaking the night from its streets. The city had not disappeared, exactly, but it had loosened its collar.

That is the first thing to understand about riding around Amsterdam. You do not have to leave the city to find space, and you do not have to plan an expedition to feel that the day has opened up. The roads become quieter by degrees. Brick gives way to trees, canal houses to dike cottages, and the familiar sound of a bicycle bell carries further than the traffic.
Here are a few places I return to when somebody asks what they should do around Amsterdam. They are not a checklist. They are ways into the city, and each one leaves enough room for a detour.
Start north of the IJ

Take the free ferry to Noord and begin at NDSM Wharf, where the old shipyard has become a place for studios, cafés, markets and large pieces of art that would never survive a planning meeting in the centre. The ride from the ferry is short, but the change is immediate. There is more sky, more wind, and a sense that the city is still deciding what it wants to become.

From there, you can continue towards the villages and polders of Waterland. The surface is mostly kind, the gradients are modest, and the landscape does the work. Wooden houses sit close to the road. Cows watch from fields behind narrow ditches. At Durgerdam, the dike runs beside the IJmeer, with the water on one side and a row of carefully kept houses on the other. Stop here for a while. A good ride should include standing still.

If you have the legs and the weather, carry on towards Marken. The former island is reached across a long dike, and the green houses seem to have been placed there by somebody who understood the value of a strong colour against a grey sky. You can make a full day of it, or turn back earlier. There is no prize for arriving tired.
Follow the water through the city
For something closer to the centre, ride east from Centraal and pick up the Amstel. The river is generous in this way. It gives you a route that feels rural without asking you to travel far.

The Magere Brug and the theatres come first, then the houses begin to thin out. Past the ring road, the path opens beside fields and the Riekermolen, a thatched windmill standing near the riverbank. The city remains close, but it no longer demands your attention. You can hear a barge engine, a bird in the reeds, the soft contact of tyres with the path.

Ouderkerk aan de Amstel makes a natural pause. Find a bench or a café, put the bike somewhere sensible and let lunch take the time it takes. The best routes around Amsterdam are measured less by distance than by the number of times you have found a reason to stop.
Make room for a park

Amsterdam has parks for different kinds of day. Vondelpark is the obvious choice for a slow loop through the city, especially early, before the paths fill with walkers and children learning to ride. Flevopark, further east, feels more local and more spacious. It is a good place to see how a city can provide ordinary access to trees, water and quiet without turning every green space into a destination.

South of the centre, Amsterdamse Bos offers a larger horizon. Its paths run through woods and open ground, past lakes and fields where the city feels pleasantly distant. You can ride there for an hour or most of a day. The point is not to conquer it. The point is to let the rhythm settle.

This is one of the quiet achievements of Dutch cycling: not speed, but proximity. The freedom to reach a forest, a river or a village from an ordinary street changes the shape of a week. It makes a small amount of time feel useful.
Ride west to the Zaan

The route to Zaanse Schans is busier in places, and the wind across the open land can be honest about its intentions. Go anyway, with patience. The working windmills and wooden houses along the Zaan are well known, but the ride towards them is the better argument for going by bicycle. You see the industrial edges, the water, the small roads and the places where the city gradually becomes countryside.

If the wind is behind you, take advantage of it. If it is not, settle into a lower gear and remember that weather is part of the country, not a personal insult. A durable bike helps, but so does carrying a repair kit and accepting that the day may take longer than expected.
Finish where the land meets the sea

For a longer outing, follow the routes through the dunes towards Zandvoort and the North Sea. The landscape changes again: pale sand, marram grass, narrow paths through the dunes and then the broad, bracing edge of the water. It is a satisfying finish because there is nowhere else for the road to go.

The Netherlands did not stumble into these connections. It chose them, street by street and path by path, after people decided that everyday journeys deserved safety, comfort and a little beauty. The legacy of Stop de Kindermoord and the steady work that followed can still be felt in the simple fact that a child, a pensioner and a workshop mechanic can all set out on the same network and make a day of it.

You will have to make allowances. Rain arrives from the side. Some routes are crowded. A headwind does not care how carefully you planned your afternoon. But these are manageable difficulties, and they are easier to accept when the alternative is a day spent moving through a place without really seeing it.

By late afternoon, I am usually back near the Amstel, with a little grit on the frame and the faint smell of woodsmoke from somewhere along the bank. Amsterdam is drawing itself together again: ferries crossing, bells sounding, people carrying bread home in front baskets. I turn towards the workshop, not in any hurry, and let the tyres find their quiet line through the evening streets.
